A1.justification: Both PDFs are readable, complete 19-page versions of the same study, including equations, seven figures, Table 1 and appendices. Added material and relocated or renumbered content can be matched reliably.

before.justification: v1 reports original toxicity, fluency and capability evaluations of SAE interventions, feature-splitting analyses, and Gemma-IT experiments in the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains these original empirical results and adds four examples of model completions judged non-fluent in Appendix C.

M1.justification: Section 3.1 replaces handcrafted toxic prompts, activation/frequency ranking and manual Neuronpedia filtering with selection of three features per layer using toxic/non-toxic activation differences on ParaDetox pairs. This substantially revises the component that identifies intervention directions. Ablation and the three steering procedures remain unchanged, although later sections still describe the earlier selection method.

E1.justification: v2 introduces ParaDetox's paired toxic/non-toxic sentences for feature identification, replacing the handcrafted toxic sequence described in v1. RealToxicityPrompts, the seven capability benchmarks and the Gemma-IT knowledge probes remain unchanged, limiting the coverage change to feature-identification data.

E2.justification: Figures 2, 5 and 7 retain the same DPO, LM-Steer, ProFS and prompting comparators. The LoRA/SFT experimental description is also retained. Newly cited methods are not added to the reported comparisons.

E3.justification: The reported feature-selection setup changes to approximately 50% of ParaDetox, comprising 10,000 pairs, with three selected features per layer instead of 3–8 after filtering. Downstream settings remain unchanged, including 1,199 RTP prompts, greedy 20-token continuations and 250 fluency samples. The PDFs do not establish that evaluations were rerun.

E4.justification: New Appendix C adds four qualitative failure cases illustrating incoherent or repetitive completions assigned fluency score 0. Existing detector comparisons, threshold sensitivity tests, feature-splitting analyses and Gemma-IT investigations are retained after appendix renumbering.

E5.justification: Both versions retain three-seed capability averages, standard-error bars, three-run fluency-judge reliability reporting, detector correlation tests and the Welch test for threshold sensitivity. Reported reliability statistics, including Krippendorff's alpha of 0.77, are unchanged.

E6.justification: Appendix C adds four concrete prompt-completion examples reported as fluency 0. Existing plotted results, numerical findings and Table 1 outputs are unchanged, including the feature-splitting toxicity gap of 0.062 and its reduction to 0.01 after mitigation. No quantitative improvement from the revised selection procedure is demonstrated.

T1.justification: The SAE encoder/decoder equations and steering updates and masks retain their mathematical content. Adding a layer index to the feature-set notation does not introduce substantive theory, assumptions or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract, principal contributions and conclusion retain the claims about SAE detoxification, three steering tiers, toxicity–fluency trade-offs, preserved benchmark capability and detrimental feature splitting. The additional introductory motivation sentence restates the existing evaluation objective.

C2.justification: Section 3.1 newly argues that meaning-preserving toxic/non-toxic pairs isolate toxicity-related activation changes and improve feature monosemanticity. Section 2.3 adds an explicit practical rationale for detoxification without refusal. Existing limitations remain, including the manual-selection limitation that conflicts with the revised method description.

D1.justification: Footnote 1 changes from a promised code release upon acceptance to a direct 'Code' repository reference, and the Neuronpedia API footnote is removed. Existing baseline hyperparameters, fluency-judge prompt, hardware and compute-cost disclosures are retained in renumbered appendices.

R1.justification: v2 adds Goyal et al. (2025), Das et al. (2025), Logacheva et al. (2022) and Wester et al. (2024), covering moderation, toxic-memory editing, ParaDetox and refusal-related user experience. It more explicitly distinguishes its goal from refusal steering while retaining the overall SAE safety positioning.

P1.justification: Changes comprise a localized rewrite of feature identification, short motivation and related-work additions, expanded acknowledgments and new Appendix C. Subsequent appendices are renumbered; the overall narrative and most prose remain intact.

P2.justification: All seven figure designs and Table 1 are retained. Reflow relocates figures and appendix material, including Figure 3 from PDF page 6 to 7 and Figure 4 from page 7 to 8, and removes printed page numbers. The two-column layout, plot axes and legends remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v1 consistently connects its feature-selection description to its results. In v2, Section 3.1 specifies ParaDetox-based selection, while Section 4.1, Appendix G and Section 8 retain frequency-based selection, maximum-activation selection and manual filtering without reconciliation. This creates uncertainty about how the features underlying the unchanged results were selected, weakening reproducibility. The useful new fluency examples and contextual additions do not offset this methodological inconsistency.
